issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategies imply a current external danger/assault-style threat context (arming oneself, hypervigilant scanning for physical threat) that is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of a child's life-threatening illness, where danger is usually medical and not mitigated by carrying a weapon or scanning for attackers.

issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: Within the profile, these threat-focused safety behaviours are not supported by any Threat items and fit poorly with the formulation, which has Triggers and Threat fully inactive; they suggest a strong trigger/threat loop that the rest of the self-report does not reflect.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: The contamination appraisal is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of a child's life-threatening illness. It is more characteristic of interpersonal/sexual trauma or moral injury and lacks support from the other selected items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
issues.explanation: Avoiding medical cues is plausible for a child's severe illness, but the additional strategies of avoiding public transport and constantly scanning for external threat suggest a danger-based trauma context not represented in the memory or appraisal items.

issues.item: Avoid Public Transport: Using public transport
issues.explanation: For trauma centered on a child's life-threatening illness, avoiding public transport is hard to link clinically unless other items indicate transport-related reminders or hospital-travel cues; no such trigger or memory content is present here, so this strategy appears context-mismatched.

issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: Constantly scanning the environment for threat implies an ongoing external danger focus, but the rest of the profile is dominated by trauma-memory disorganisation and self-change appraisals rather than current external-threat concerns. With Threat and Trigger links inactive, this item sits awkwardly in the formulation.

issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: This item is hard to reconcile with the trauma type (child's life-threatening illness) and the rest of the profile. The selected appraisals and memory items center on traumatic recollection, permanent change, and distrust, but not on a current external danger context. 'Constantly scan environment for signs of threat' implies hypervigilance for immediate environmental threat, which is more characteristic of assault/combat-type trauma and is not clinically linked here given that all Triggers and Threat edges are inactive in the formulation. It also sits poorly with the other maladaptive strategies, which are illness/trauma-processing related (avoid care, suppress thoughts).

vignette: Minh is a 69-year-old Vietnamese American man who works as a nanny, a role he took on after his wife died, to stay connected to the energy of young children. Two years ago, while caring for three-year-old Leo, the son of a neighbor, Minh watched the boy suddenly seize during a high fever. He called 911, but in the minutes before the ambulance arrived he could do nothing but hold Leo as the child's body stiffened and his eyes rolled back. The diagnosis was bacterial meningitis; Leo survived after weeks in the ICU. Minh stopped telling the story after a few attempts because he could never get the sequence straight-the timeline felt scrambled, the details shifting-and the few times he tried, the memory would flood him with such sensory force that his hands would tremble and his chest would tighten as if he were back in that living room. He had come to believe that the person he was before that afternoon no longer existed; the man who had felt competent and calm with children had been replaced by someone who startled at a child's cough and who saw hidden threats in ordinary faces. That sense of being permanently damaged, of having crossed a line he could not uncross, made the memory feel less like a recollection and more like a trap he was still living inside. Through the months that followed, Minh developed a private rhythm of survival. He tried hard not to think about Leo's seizure or the hospital, but the more he pushed the memory away, the more it erupted with vivid, present-tense clarity-the smell of Leo's skin, the pitch of his mother's scream, the blue of the paramedic's gloves. He kept his mind occupied constantly: crossword puzzles, long bus rides, cooking elaborate meals he barely ate. And he began to avoid medical settings altogether. When Leo's mother asked Minh to accompany them to a follow-up pediatric appointment, he invented a stomachache and stayed home. He stopped getting his own blood pressure checked, telling himself the numbers would only confirm what he already knew: that something inside him had broken irreparably. Minh's distrust of others grew quietly but steadily; he noticed the way people's eyes slid away when he spoke about the event, and he became certain they were hiding their judgment of his failure. This distrust reinforced the memory's power-if he could not trust others to tell him the truth, then the only reality he could rely on was the one that played in his mind, and that reality insisted the event was still happening. In turn, the intrusive, present-tense memory confirmed his belief that he had permanently changed: how could he be the same person if his past felt more alive than his present? He found himself unable to form a coherent narrative of what had happened, not just to the emergency room staff right after, but even to himself alone at night. The fragments would not arrange themselves into a story with a beginning, middle, and end; they stayed as isolated, unbearable moments. Suppressing those moments only made them sharper, and the cycle tightened. At work, Minh now avoids taking care of any child who shows the slightest sign of illness, even a sniffle, and he has begun turning down families with toddlers, the age Leo was. He tells his supervisor he is tired, but the truth is that a feverish child triggers a cascade of vivid, physical memory that leaves him drenched in sweat and unable to speak. His avoidance of medical care almost cost him his own health when he ignored chest pains for three weeks, attributing them to age rather than the panic his body was holding. What finally brought Minh to a therapist was a moment three weeks ago: he was pushing a stroller through the park and a toddler on a blanket coughed-a small, ordinary sound-and Minh's vision went gray. He dropped to his knees, convinced Leo was seizing again, and did not recognize the child's mother trying to help him up. He came home that evening and sat in the dark, unable to name who he had become. He is terrified that he will never be able to hold a crying child again without collapsing inside, but he is more frightened that if he does not change course, the man he used to be will vanish entirely, leaving only this trembling stranger in his place.
